title: Influence of Pilot-Scale Spray and Freeze Drying on the Compositional, Structural, and Functional Properties of Rapeseed Protein Concentrate
content: Rapeseed (Brassica napus L.) press cake, a side stream of oil production, has gained in-terest as a source of functional protein. While press cake processing, protein extraction, and drying have been studied at laboratory scale, their behavior at industry-relevant scale needs further investigation, and a systematic comparison of pilot-scale spray and freeze drying of rapeseed protein concentrate (RPC) is lacking. This study therefore compared spray- and freeze-dried RPC (SD-RPC, FD-RPC) produced at pilot scale, re-garding their composition, color, secondary structure (FTIR), molecular weight distri-bution (SDS-PAGE), particle size, zeta potential, solubility, and techno-functional properties. Results showed that the drying method did not significantly influence pro-tein chemistry, including protein composition, secondary structure, and isoelectric point (~pH 3.5). Physical properties, in contrast, differed significantly: freeze drying resulted in coarser, bimodally distributed particles with lower residual moisture, while spray drying produced finer, monomodal particles with a lighter color. These differences were reflected in the techno-functional behavior, where FD-RPC showed significantly higher water/oil holding and emulsion capacity, while emulsion stability, foaming, and least gelation concentration were comparable. Spray drying proved a feasible, scalable al-ternative, yielding a concentrate with comparable protein chemistry yet distinct physical functionality, promising for emulsion- and gel-based food applications.
